Evolutionary Architecture — Fitness Functions and Technical Debt

This lesson introduces evolutionary architecture as a disciplined approach to building systems that can change safely over time — a critical capability for long-lived financial platforms.

Why Architecture Must Evolve

No financial system is designed once and left unchanged. Regulatory mandates arrive unexpectedly. Acquisition targets must be integrated. Traffic patterns shift with product launches. The systems that survive at scale are not the ones with the most carefully planned initial design — they are the ones built to absorb change without breaking.

The CAP Theorem — Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance
documents.body:
The CAP Theorem — Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance

The CAP theorem is the foundational constraint of distributed systems. Every architectural decision in a distributed financial system is a trade-off that CAP — and its more nuanced successor, PACELC — helps you reason about.

The Theorem

In 2000, Eric Brewer conjectured, and Gilbert and Lynch later proved, that a distributed data store can provide at most two of the following three guarantees simultaneously:

- Consistency (C) — Every read receives the most recent write or an error. All nodes see the same data at the same time.
- Availability (A) — Every request receives a response (not an error), though the response may not contain the most recent write.
- Partition Tolerance (P) — The system continues operating even when network messages between nodes are lost or delayed.

The choice is not "pick 2 of 3" in practice. Network partitions will occur in any distributed system. Therefore the real choice is: when a partition happens, do you sacrifice consistency or availability?

Why Partition Tolerance Is Not Optional

A network partition is any scenario where nodes cannot communicate:

- A network cable is cut between data centres
- A switch fails under load
- A noisy neighbour saturates a network interface
- A cloud provider has a BGP routing incident

In any system spanning more than one process (which includes every distributed financial system), you must tolerate partitions. The P in CAP is therefore not a choice — it is a requirement.

The real choice is CP vs AP: what do you do during a partition?

CP Systems — Consistency Over Availability

CP systems refuse to respond when they cannot guarantee the response is current. They prioritise correctness over uptime.

Examples: HBase, MongoDB (with majority write concern), etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul

- Account balance reads during a payment authorisation

The Java Memory Model — Fundamentals
documents.body:
Overview

The Java Memory Model (JMM) is the specification that defines how the Java Virtual Machine interacts with the computer's memory system. It answers a fundamental question every concurrent Java programmer must understand:

If Thread 1 writes a value to a variable, is Thread 2 guaranteed to see that new value?

The answer — without synchronization — is no. Understanding why leads directly to understanding every class of data race, lost update, and financial consistency failure that occurs in production financial systems.

This lesson establishes the foundation that every subsequent concurrency topic builds upon.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Explain what the JMM defines and why it exists
- Describe the difference between main memory and thread working memory
- Identify the visibility problem and explain its root cause
- Define the happens-before relationship and list its sources
- Correctly apply to solve visibility problems
- Explain why is insufficient for compound operations
- Describe how the JMM applies to virtual threads in Java 21

Business Context

A payment processing system receives 8,000 withdrawal requests per second. Each request is handled by a separate thread. The account balance is a shared mutable field.

Thread 1 debits £200 from an account with balance £1,000. Thread 2 reads the balance 10 microseconds later to determine if a £900 withdrawal is permitted.

Without correct JMM awareness: Thread 2 may read the stale value £1,000 — the debit by Thread 1 is simply invisible to it. Thread 2 approves the £900 withdrawal. The account is now overdrawn by £100. No exception was thrown. No lock was violated. The system behaved exactly as coded — incorrectly.

This is not a hypothetical. Lost updates in banking systems caused by JMM ignorance have resulted in real overdrafts, compliance failures, and regulatory fines. The JMM is not an academic curiosity. It is the first line of financial data correctness.

documents.body:
Overview

Thread safety is a property of code: a class or method is thread-safe if it behaves correctly when accessed from multiple threads simultaneously, without requiring any additional synchronisation from the caller.

The best thread-safe code requires no synchronisation at all — it achieves safety through design, not locks. Understanding the hierarchy of thread-safety strategies lets you choose the right approach for every situation and avoid reaching for synchronisation when simpler solutions exist.

This lesson covers the three fundamental strategies — immutability, stateless design, and thread confinement — and shows how Java 17 and 21 features make each strategy easier to implement correctly.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Identify and apply the three primary thread-safety strategies
- Design immutable value objects correctly using fields and Java records
- Distinguish stateless services from stateful ones and explain why stateless is safer
- Apply thread confinement via local variables, , and stack confinement
- Explain why fields provide safe publication guarantees
- Recognise and eliminate common thread-safety mistakes in financial service code
- Choose the appropriate strategy for a given concurrency scenario

Business Context

A payment processing platform handles 12,000 requests per second across 200 virtual threads. The engineering team is onboarding three junior engineers who keep introducing subtle thread-safety bugs:

- A with a mutable exchange-rate cache gets partially updated when two threads write simultaneously, producing garbled rates
- A stores intermediate results in an instance field, causing two threads processing different transactions to corrupt each other's calculations
- A using a shared throws under load because is not thread-safe

Each incident requires a production rollback. The team needs a principled framework for making code thread-safe by design, not by accident.

Double-Entry Ledger — Architecture and Invariants
documents.body:
Overview

Every financial system — from a startup's payment API to a central bank's real-time gross settlement system — is built on a 700-year-old idea: double-entry bookkeeping. Every transaction touches at least two accounts, with debits always equalling credits. The sum never lies.

This lesson establishes the theoretical and technical foundation of ledger design. It covers the accounting equation, T-accounts, journal entry semantics, database schema design, and the architectural constraints that keep a ledger correct under concurrent load. Everything in this track — race conditions, idempotency, outbox patterns, saga compensation — exists to protect the invariants introduced here.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- State the accounting equation and explain its significance as a system invariant
- Describe debit and credit semantics for each account type
- Read and write journal entries in both accounting notation and SQL
- Design a minimal double-entry ledger database schema
- Implement balance calculation as a SQL aggregate over the journal
- Explain why append-only design is preferred for financial ledgers

2. Engineers posting a debit without a corresponding credit — breaking the fundamental invariant and causing the general ledger to be out of balance

documents.body:
Overview

The lost update problem is the most financially damaging class of concurrency bug. Two concurrent transactions both read the same account balance, both decide the balance is sufficient, and both proceed with a withdrawal. The result: the account is overdrawn by the full amount of one withdrawal. Neither transaction detected an error. No exception was thrown. The system behaved as coded — incorrectly.

This scenario traces the problem from first principles, shows the broken implementation, explains why it breaks, and walks through three correct solutions with different trade-off profiles. By the end, you will have the technical vocabulary, implementation knowledge, and decision criteria to prevent overdrafts in any concurrent financial system.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Identify and explain the lost update pattern in a database read-modify-write cycle
- Explain why MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) does not prevent lost updates at READ COMMITTED
- Implement pessimistic locking using in SQL and JPA
- Implement optimistic locking using a version column and in JPA
- Implement atomic conditional SQL UPDATE as a lock-free alternative
- Choose the correct strategy based on contention, latency, and consistency requirements
- Write a jcstress test to detect a concurrent withdrawal race condition

documents.title: Scenario B — Duplicate Payment Detection and Idempotency
documents.body:
Overview

Idempotency means that performing the same operation multiple times produces the same result as performing it once. In financial systems, this is not an optional enhancement — it is a correctness requirement. Networks are unreliable. Clients time out and retry. Message queues deliver at-least-once. Without idempotency, a timeout followed by a retry doubles the charge.

This scenario covers the full problem space: why duplicate payments occur, how idempotency keys work, the check-then-act race condition in naive implementations, and how database constraints provide the only reliable deduplication guarantee. By the end, your payment services will be safe to retry from any client, in any network condition.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Explain why idempotency is a correctness requirement in distributed payment systems
- Design an idempotency key scheme for HTTP APIs and message consumers
- Implement idempotent payment posting using a database UNIQUE constraint
- Explain and prevent the check-then-act race condition in concurrent duplicate requests
- Handle the UNIQUE constraint violation correctly to return a consistent response
- Implement idempotent Kafka consumers using offset-based and key-based deduplication
- Choose between client-generated and server-generated idempotency keys

A payment API serves both a mobile app and a web frontend. Under load, the mobile app's HTTP client has an aggressive retry policy: if it receives no response within 3 seconds, it retries the request automatically, up to 3 times.

SLOs and Error Budgets — Reliability Engineering for Finance

Service Level Objectives are the foundational contract of reliability engineering. In financial systems, they translate vague "high availability" requirements into measurable, actionable engineering goals.

The SLI → SLO → SLA Hierarchy

Service Level Indicator (SLI) — A quantitative measure of service behaviour. The raw metric.

Service Level Objective (SLO) — A target range for an SLI. The engineering goal.

JVM Internals — Memory Model, Class Loading, and JIT

Understanding JVM internals is prerequisite to meaningful performance engineering. Without a mental model of how Java allocates memory, compiles code, and manages threads, you are guessing at optimisations.

The JVM Memory Model

The JVM partitions memory into distinct regions, each with different lifecycle and garbage collection behaviour.

Heap Regions — Where Your Objects Live

Eden Space — New objects are allocated here. Fast bump-pointer allocation. Collected frequently (Minor GC).

Survivor Spaces (S0/S1) — Objects that survive Minor GC are moved here. Copied between S0 and S1 on each Minor GC. Objects are promoted to Old Generation after a configurable number of GC cycles (default: 15 for G1GC).

Old Generation (Tenured) — Long-lived objects. Collected less frequently (Major/Full GC). The primary source of GC pause latency in financial systems.

Metaspace — Class metadata (method descriptors, field metadata, bytecode). Unlike PermGen (removed in Java 8), Metaspace grows dynamically and is bounded by . Class loader leaks cause Metaspace OOM.

Object Allocation — What Happens When You Write 

1. TLAB allocation (Thread-Local Allocation Buffer) — Each thread has a private chunk of Eden to allocate into without synchronisation. does a simple pointer bump within the TLAB — essentially free.

2. If TLAB is full — Request a new TLAB from Eden. If Eden is full → trigger Minor GC.

3. Large object handling — Objects exceeding a threshold () are allocated directly into Old Generation, skipping Eden entirely. This is a performance trap for large buffers common in payment message parsing.

Garbage Collection — G1GC and ZGC

G1GC — The Default for Financial Systems (Java 9+)

G1 (Garbage First) divides the heap into equal-sized regions (~1-32MB). It aims to meet a configurable pause time goal by collecting the regions with the most garbage first (hence "Garbage First").

ACID Properties — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability

ACID is not an abstract academic concept — it is the operational foundation of financial data integrity. Every transaction your system processes relies on these guarantees. Principal engineers must be able to reason about what happens when each one is violated.

Why ACID Matters for Financial Systems

Consider a money transfer: debit £500 from Account A, credit £500 to Account B.

Without ACID:
- Without Atomicity — debit succeeds, credit fails → £500 disappears from the system
- Without Consistency — total money in the system changes after the transfer
- Without Isolation — another transaction reads Account A as £500 lower mid-transfer, before Account B is credited
- Without Durability — the transfer succeeds, but a crash before disk flush loses it

Atomicity — All or Nothing

An atomic transaction either completes fully or has no effect at all. There is no partial state.

Atomicity Implementation — PostgreSQL WAL

PostgreSQL implements atomicity through the Write-Ahead Log (WAL). Before any data page is modified, the change is written to the WAL. If the database crashes mid-transaction:

1. On restart, PostgreSQL reads the WAL
2. Completed transactions (with COMMIT record) are replayed
3. Incomplete transactions (no COMMIT) are rolled back

The WAL provides the crash recovery guarantee — no partially-committed transactions survive a crash.

Consistency — Valid State Transitions

Consistency guarantees that a transaction transforms the database from one valid state to another valid state. It relies on constraints, triggers, and application logic working together.

Consistency is partly your responsibility. The database enforces structural constraints (CHECK, FOREIGN KEY), but business consistency rules must be implemented in application code. A constraint won't protect you from a race condition where two concurrent reads both see sufficient balance.

Kafka Architecture — Topics, Partitions, and Consumer Groups

Apache Kafka is the dominant messaging platform in financial services — not because it's simple, but because it provides the combination of durability, throughput, and replay capability that event-driven financial systems require. This lesson builds the architectural mental model needed to use Kafka correctly.

Why Kafka Exists — The Problem It Solves

Traditional message queues (RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ) delete messages after consumption. This creates a fundamental problem for financial systems:

- Replay — if a consumer has a bug, you cannot re-process historical events
- Multiple consumers — adding a new service (analytics, compliance) requires a separate queue copy
- Throughput — queue-based systems struggle beyond ~100k messages/second
- Ordering — delivery ordering guarantees conflict with high availability

- Parallelism — consumers process partitions concurrently

Your team is on-call for a challenger bank's payment platform. At 02:14, PagerDuty fires: account balance monitoring reports 23 accounts with negative balances. No overdraft facility has been granted. You pull up the logs.

Fix with SELECT FOR UPDATE to serialise concurrent access to the same account row. Race condition in read-modify-write cycle (lost update). Customer service has escalated 50 double-charge complaints in the past week. Investigation shows: mobile app clients use an aggressive retry policy — if no response within 3 seconds, they retry up to 3 times. Under load, the payment service occasionally takes 4–6 seconds to respond.

The current idempotency implementation checks for an existing payment by idempotency key before inserting. The idempotency key is a UUID generated by the client before the first attempt. The current code uses: (1) SELECT payment WHERE idempotency_key = ?, (2) if found, return existing result, (3) if not found, INSERT new payment and process. What is the fundamental flaw in this approach? The idempotency key should be generated server-side. Client-generated keys cannot be trusted and may collide across different clients. The SELECT and INSERT are two separate operations with a race window between them. Two concurrent retries can both pass the SELECT check (finding nothing) before either commits the INSERT. Both then insert, creating duplicate payments. The SELECT query needs a row-level lock (SELECT FOR UPDATE) to prevent concurrent reads from seeing the same empty result. The 24-hour expiry on idempotency keys is too short. Keys should be permanent to prevent customers from accidentally re-initiating payments after key expiry. What should the service return to the client? HTTP 409 Conflict — the request conflicts with existing state. The client should handle this as a recoverable error. What is causing the Full GC events, and why do they only occur during market-open load? G1GC's MaxGCPauseMillis target (200ms default) is too aggressive. G1GC is spending too much time trying to meet the pause target, triggering Full GC as a fallback when it cannot keep up. documents.body:
An FX trading system enforces a £500,000 maximum exposure per trader per currency pair per day. The enforcement logic: SELECT SUM(amount) FROM fx_positions WHERE trader_id = ? AND currency_pair = ? AND trade_date = TODAY. If sum + new_trade_amount <= 500,000, allow the trade and INSERT into fx_positions.

At 10:03:17.421, two traders at different desks simultaneously submit GBP/USD trades of £450,000 each. Both read exposure = £0. Both pass the check. Both trades are inserted. Net exposure: £900,000, breaching the £500,000 limit by £400,000. The compliance team is alerted at 10:04. No application error was logged. What type of concurrency anomaly caused this breach, and why did SELECT...FOR UPDATE fail to prevent it? Lost update: both transactions read £0 exposure and both wrote £450,000. This is the same race condition as the overdraft scenario — fix with an atomic conditional UPDATE. Phantom read: both transactions read the aggregate (SUM = £0) on a range of rows (WHERE trader_id = X AND currency_pair = Y AND trade_date = TODAY). At READ COMMITTED, each SELECT sees only committed data at the moment of execution — not the entire transaction's snapshot. SELECT...FOR UPDATE acquires no lock because there are no rows matching the WHERE clause at read time. When Transaction 1 commits its £450k INSERT, Transaction 2's already-completed SELECT is not re-evaluated. Dirty read: Transaction 2 read Transaction 1's uncommitted £450,000 insert, but due to a database bug, the read returned £0 instead of the correct pending value. Network partition between the two application pods caused both to miss each other's in-progress transactions. What is the correct isolation level fix, and what is the trade-off you must manage in production? Use REPEATABLE READ isolation. This prevents phantom reads by taking a snapshot at transaction start. Use SERIALIZABLE isolation with retry logic: PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE uses SSI (Serialisable Snapshot Isolation) to detect read-write conflicts.…

At 14:22, a customer submits a £1,200 rent payment. The request times out after 28 seconds (mobile app timeout). The app displays an error. The mobile app sent different Idempotency-Key values despite displaying the same UUID to the developer. A client-side UUID generation bug produced two different keys. documents.title: The Database Migration Deadline
documents.subtitle: Zero-Downtime Column Addition on an 800 Million Row Table
documents.body:
The compliance team requires a new `risk_score NUMERIC(5,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00` column on the `payment_transactions` table. The table has 800 million rows and receives 20,000 inserts per second.

The DBA estimates the naive ALTER TABLE will take 6 hours (full table rewrite, exclusive lock held throughout). Business has approved a Saturday maintenance window of 15 minutes. Product says any longer window is unacceptable due to PSD2 real-time payment requirements.

Engineering must deliver the column addition before next Wednesday's regulatory audit. Why does `ALTER TABLE payment_transactions ADD COLUMN risk_score NUMERIC(5,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00` take 6 hours, and what lock does it hold? PostgreSQL must verify the NOT NULL constraint by scanning all 800M rows. The constraint check takes approximately 400 seconds at 2M rows/second, holding a ShareLock that allows reads but blocks writes. Adding a NOT NULL column with a constant DEFAULT requires PostgreSQL to rewrite every row in the table to include the new column value. 800M rows × ~50 bytes per row rewrite = ~40GB written. At typical I/O rates (100MB/s write), this takes 400 seconds minimum, plus index rebuilds and checkpoint overhead. An ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock is held for the entire duration — blocking all reads and writes. The operation requires stopping replication to all read replicas while the table is being modified, then resyncing the replicas from scratch after the modification completes. PostgreSQL must rebuild all existing indexes on the table to incorporate the new column into the index metadata, even if the new column is not indexed. What is the correct zero-downtime migration strategy for this column addition? Use pg_repack to perform an online table rebuild: creates a new table with the extra column, copies rows in background, swaps old table with new atomically. documents.subtitle: Dual-Write Failure Leaves £3.2M in Payments Unprocessed
documents.body:
Payment service flow: (1) validate payment, (2) commit to PostgreSQL (`payment_transactions` table), (3) publish `payment.authorised` event to Kafka for downstream settlement processing.

After a Friday deployment, monitoring shows 847 payments committed to PostgreSQL but no corresponding Kafka events. Settlement service lag counter reads 0 — it has not consumed any new events in 4 hours. £3.2M in authorised payments have not been submitted for settlement.

The Kafka broker logs show no errors. The payment service logs show Kafka producer errors for a 12-minute window (14:03–14:15) on Friday — during which a broker restarted — then healthy publishing resumed. The 847 unprocessed payments all fall within that 12-minute window. What is the fundamental architectural problem that caused the 847 missing events? The Kafka broker restart caused the payment service's producer to reconnect. During reconnection, the in-flight send() calls were silently dropped. The dual-write problem: the PostgreSQL commit and the Kafka publish are two independent operations with no atomicity guarantee. The commit succeeded; the Kafka publish failed (broker restart). These two writes cannot be wrapped in a distributed transaction. Without the Transactional Outbox pattern, there is no way to guarantee that a committed payment always produces a Kafka event. The settlement service's Kafka auto-commit advanced past the missing events. The events were published but marked as consumed before settlement processing completed. The Kafka topic's retention period expired for the 14:03-14:15 events before the settlement service could consume them. What is the correct architectural fix to prevent this recurrence? Use Kafka's exactly-once semantics (enable.idempotence=true + transactional.id). Wrap the PostgreSQL commit and Kafka publish in a Kafka transaction. documents.subtitle: JVM OOM from Unbounded Cache Accumulating PDF Byte Arrays
documents.body:
Payment gateway pods restart every 4–6 hours with OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. This started exactly 3 weeks ago after releasing a new PDF statement generation feature. Normal pod memory usage: 400MB. Pods restart at ~3.8GB heap used.

The team increased -Xmx from 2GB to 4GB two weeks ago, which extended pod lifetime from 2 hours to 4-6 hours without fixing the underlying issue. Kubernetes liveness probes restart pods on OOM, so availability is maintained (new pod starts in ~45 seconds). However, restarts coincide with peak transaction hours, causing elevated latency. Before analysing the heap dump, what is the most likely root cause based on the symptoms alone? The PDF generation library has a native memory leak. It allocates off-heap memory via JNI that the JVM garbage collector cannot reclaim. The PDF feature populates a cache (likely a static Map or Spring @Cacheable bean) with the generated PDF byte[] data, keyed by accountId. The cache has no eviction policy or size limit. Every statement request adds ~2MB of byte[] to the cache. After 3 weeks of usage, the cache has grown to consume all available heap. GC cannot collect the byte[] because the cache holds strong references. HTTP session objects from PDF download requests are accumulating in memory. Each PDF download session is not being invalidated, holding a reference to the byte[] response body. The PDF generation creates a new ClassLoader per request to isolate the PDF library. documents.body:
The payment processing team receives 420 PagerDuty pages in one week. 65% are P2 alerts for P99 latency > 500ms. P50 latency is healthy at 45ms. P99 is naturally spiky — GC pauses and 1–2% of slow downstream API calls push individual requests above 500ms even during normal operation.

Engineers begin muting P99 alerts during business hours. On Wednesday afternoon, a genuine 25-minute partial outage (40% of payments timing out) goes undetected for 25 minutes because the alert was lost in the noise. Customers escalate via Twitter. The engineering VP asks for a root-cause analysis of the monitoring failure. What is the fundamental flaw in the current alerting strategy that causes both the false positive storm and the missed real outage? The P99 threshold (500ms) is too aggressive. Raising it to 2,000ms would eliminate the false positives and would have caught the genuine outage. Point-in-time threshold alerts fire on transient spikes that self-resolve without consuming meaningful error budget. A 1-minute P99 spike to 600ms consumes 1 minute of the 43.8-minute monthly budget but generates a PagerDuty page. Genuine outages also spike P99 — but they burn budget continuously. Alerting on P50 (median) latency would have fewer false positives because the median is more stable. Too many teams are subscribed to the same alert. Alert routing should ensure only the on-call engineer is paged, reducing the perception of noise. What alerting strategy should replace the point-in-time P99 threshold alert? The monthly billing job runs fine in staging: 50,000 customers, completes in 4 minutes. First production run with 8.2 million customers has been running for 6 hours without completing. The core query:

```sql
SELECT c.id, c.email, SUM(t.amount) as total_billed
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN transactions t ON c.id = t.customer_id
WHERE t.created_at >= '2026-10-01'
  AND c.billing_status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY c.id, c.email
```

The payments API v1 has been live for 18 months. It returns:
